Total isolation game in graphs

Affiliation: Michael A. Henning and Affiliation: Douglas F. Rall Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Applied MathematicsUniversity of JohannesburgAuckland Park, 2006 South AfricaEmail: mahenning@uj.ac.za Affiliation: Professor Emeritus of MathematicsFurman UniversityGreenville, SC, USAEmail: doug.rall@furman.edu
Abstract

The total isolation game is played on a graph GG by two players who take turns playing a vertex such that if SS is the set of already played vertices, then a vertex can be selected only if it is adjacent to a vertex that belongs to a (nontrivial) component of the graph G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) of order at least 22 or a vertex that is isolated in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) and belongs to the set SS, where NG​(S)N_{G}(S) is the set of vertices adjacent to a vertex in SS. Dominator wishes to finish the game with the minimum number of played vertices, while Staller has the opposite goal. The game total isolation number ιgt​(G)\iota_{\rm gt}(G) is the number of moves in the Dominator-start game where both players play optimally. We prove that if GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3, then ιgt​(G)<56​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)<\frac{5}{6}n. Furthermore if GG has minimum degree at least 22, then we prove that ιgt​(G)≤34​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{3}{4}n. More generally, if GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then we prove that ιgt​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n. Among other results it is proved that if GG is a graph of order nn with diameter 22, then ιgt​(G)≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n.

Keywords: Total isolating set; total isolation game; domination; total domination
AMS subject classification: 05C65, 05C69

1 Introduction

A vertex uu in a graph GG dominates a vertex vv if u=vu=v or uu is adjacent to vv in GG. A dominating set of GG is a set SS of vertices of GG such that every vertex in GG is dominated by a vertex in SS. A vertex uu in a graph GG totally dominates a vertex vv if uu is adjacent to vv in GG. A total dominating set of GG is a set SS of vertices of GG such that every vertex of GG is totally dominated by a vertex in SS. Thus, a set SS is a dominating set of GG if every vertex in V⁡(G)∖SV(G)\setminus S is adjacent to at least one vertex in SS, and a set SS is a total dominating set of GG if every vertex is adjacent to at least one vertex in SS. The concept of domination and its variations have been widely studied in theoretical, algorithmic and application aspects. A thorough treatment of (total) domination in graphs and its variants can be found in the books [14, 15].

The open neighborhood of a vertex vv in GG is the set of neighbors of vv, denoted NG​(v)N_{G}(v), where two vertices are neighbors if they are adjacent. Thus, NG​(v)={u∈V⁡(G):u​v∈E⁡(G)}N_{G}(v)=\{u\in V(G)\,\colon uv\in E(G)\}. The closed neighborhood of vv is the set NG​[v]=NG​(v)∪{v}N_{G}[v]=N_{G}(v)\cup\{v\}. The open neighborhood of a set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is the set of all neighbors of vertices in SS, denoted NG​(S)N_{G}(S), whereas the closed neighborhood of SS is NG​[S]=NG​(S)∪SN_{G}[S]=N_{G}(S)\cup S. Thus,

NG​(S)=⋃v∈SNG​(v)andNG​[S]=⋃v∈SNG​[v].N_{G}(S)=\bigcup_{v\in S}N_{G}(v)\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{and}\hskip 14.22636ptN_{G}[S]=\bigcup_{v\in S}N_{G}[v].

A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is an isolating set of GG if removing SS and its neighborhood NG​(S)N_{G}(S) leaves no edge, that is, V​(G)∖NG​[S]V(G)\setminus N_{G}[S] is an independent set in GG. The concept was introduced (in a more general setting) in 2017 by Caro and Hansberg [11]. The isolation number ι⁡(G)\iota(G) of GG is the minimum cardinality among all isolating sets of GG. This parameter is equivalent to the vertex-edge domination number, introduced earlier by Peters [18]. Isolation in graphs is studied further, for example, in [1, 3, 10, 12, 13, 17, 19].

A total isolating set is an isolating set SS with the additional property that the subgraph G⁡[S]G[S] induced by SS contains no vertex of degree 00. The total isolation number ιt​(G)\iota^{t}(G) of GG is the minimum cardinality among all total isolating sets of GG. This parameter was originally introduced by Boutrig and Chellali [2] as the total vertex-edge domination number, and was subsequently studied, for example, in [4, 5, 10].

In 2010 Brešar, Klavžar, and Rall [8] published the seminal paper on the domination game which belongs to the growing family of competitive optimization graph games. Domination games played on graphs are now very well studied in the literature. The subsequent rapid growth by the scientific community of research on domination games played on graphs inspired the recent book entitled “Domination games played on graphs” by Brešar, Henning, Klavžar, and Rall [7], which presented the state of the art results at the time and shows that the area is rich for further research. In this paper, we study the total version of the isolation game in graphs.

Recently Brešar, Dravec, Johnston, Kuenzel, and Rall in [6], introduced a game counterpart of the isolation number, called the isolation game, following the ideas of the classical domination game [8]. The isolation game was subsequently studied further in [9] at the Workshop on Games on Graphs III, held in Rogla, Slovenia, in June 2025. In this paper, we introduce and study a game counterpart of the total isolation number.

The total isolation game is played on a graph GG by Dominator and Staller, who take turns selecting/playing a vertex from GG while obeying the rule that if SS is the set of already played vertices, then a vertex vv can be selected only if vv totally dominates a vertex uu that belongs to a (nontrivial) component of the graph G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) of order at least 22 or vv totally dominates a vertex u∈Su\in S that is isolated in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S). Such a vertex vv is playable, and a move selecting vv is legal. The game ends when no playable vertex exists. When the game ends, the set of vertices selected forms a total isolating set of GG.

As in the domination game, in the total isolation game Dominator wishes to finish the game by playing the fewest number of vertices, while Staller wishes to delay the process as much as possible. Thus, Dominator seeks to minimize the size of the chosen set while Staller tries to make it as large as possible. If Dominator starts the game, we speak of a D-game, otherwise it is an S-game. The game total isolation number, ιgt​(G)\iota_{\rm gt}(G), and the Staller-start game total isolation number, ιgt′​(G)\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G), are the number of vertices selected in the D-game and the S-game, respectively, provided that both players play optimally.

For graph theory notation and terminology, we generally follow [14]. Specifically, let GG be a graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G), and of order n⁡(G)=|V⁡(G)|n(G)=|V(G)| and size m⁡(G)=|E⁡(G)|m(G)=|E(G)|. We denote the degree of a vertex vv in GG by degG⁡(v)\deg_{G}(v). The minimum and maximum degrees in GG are denoted by δ⁡(G)\delta(G) and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G), respectively. An isolated vertex in GG is a vertex of degree 00 in GG. A graph is isolate-free if it contains no isolated vertex. A set XX is a packing in GG if for any two distinct vertices u,v∈Xu,v\in X, we have dG​(u,v)≥3d_{G}(u,v)\geq 3, and so NG​[u]∩NG​[v]=∅N_{G}[u]\cap N_{G}[v]=\emptyset.

A trivial graph is the graph of order 11, and a nontrivial graph has order at least 22. A cycle on nn vertices is denoted by CnC_{n} and a path on nn vertices by PnP_{n}. The complete graph on nn vertices is denoted by KnK_{n}. For a subset SS of vertices of a graph GG, we denote by G−SG-S the graph obtained from GG by deleting the vertices in SS and all edges incident with vertices in SS. If S={v}S=\{v\}, then we simply write G−vG-v rather than G−{v}G-\{v\}. The subgraph induced by the set SS is denoted by G⁡[S]G[S]. The diameter of GG, denoted diam⁡(G){\rm diam}(G), is the maximum distance among all pairs of vertices in GG.

2 Continuation Principle

One of the main tools in analyzing the domination game is the Continuation Principle first presented by Kinnersley, West, and Zamani [16]. An important consequence of the Continuation Principle for a given game variant of the domination game is the fundamental property that the number of moves in the D-game and the S-game when played optimally can differ by at most 11. It is known, for example, that the Continuation Principle holds for the total domination game. And as a special case of a more general result, the authors in [6] proved that the Continuation Principle holds in the isolation game.

Consider the total isolation game played on a path P5P_{5}. Let GG be the path P5P_{5} given by v1​v2​v3​v4​v5v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}v_{4}v_{5}. In the D-game, Dominator plays as his first move the central vertex v3v_{3}, and so the set of played vertices immediately after Dominator’s first move is S={v3}S=\{v_{3}\}. We note that no component of G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) is nontrivial and that the vertex v3v_{3} is the only isolated vertex in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) that belongs to the set SS. Hence the only legal move available to Staller is either to play the vertex v2v_{2} or the vertex v4v_{4} in order to totally dominate the vertex v3v_{3}. Once Staller plays her first move (either v2v_{2} or v4v_{4}), the game is complete. Hence, ιgt​(G)=2\iota_{\rm gt}(G)=2. In the S-game, Staller plays as her first move the leaf v1v_{1}. If Dominator plays v2v_{2} on his first move, then Staller responds by playing v5v_{5}. If Dominator plays v3v_{3} on his first move, then Staller responds by playing v4v_{4}. If Dominator plays v4v_{4} on his first move, then Staller responds by playing v5v_{5}. If Dominator plays v5v_{5} on his first move, then Staller responds by playing v4v_{4}. In all four cases, one additional move is required by Dominator to complete the game. Hence, ιgt′​(G)≥4\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\geq 4. (One can show that four moves always suffice to complete the S-game, implying that ιgt′​(G)=4\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)=4, but we do not need this stronger property here.) Therefore, |ιgt​(G)−ιgt′​(G)|≥2|\iota_{\rm gt}(G)-\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)|\geq 2.

Since the total isolation game combines the flavor of the total domination game and the isolation game, and since the Continuation Principle holds for both these games, one might expect that the Continuation Principle holds for the total isolation game. If this were the case, then for every isolate-free graph GG we would have the desirable property that |ιgt​(G)−ιgt′​(G)|≤1|\iota_{\rm gt}(G)-\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)|\leq 1. However, since there are graphs GG for which |ιgt​(G)−ιgt′​(G)|>1|\iota_{\rm gt}(G)-\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)|>1, we infer the following result.

Observation 1

The Continuation Principle does not hold for the total isolation game.

3 Upper bounds for given minimum degree

We remark that the Continuation Principle is a powerful tool for establishing upper bounds on game domination type parameters, including game domination number, the game total domination number, the game isolation number, to name games where the Continuation Principle holds. However for several variants of the domination games, such as the independent domination game and the connected domination game, in which the Continuation Principle does not hold, it has proved challenging to find good upper bounds on the associated game parameters. Observation 1 therefore suggests that finding good upper bounds on the game total isolation number is likely to be a difficult problem. In this section, our aim is to provide upper bounds on the game total isolation number in terms of the minimum degree of the graph.

During the course of the total isolation game, if SS is the set of selected vertices played to date, then a vertex vv is considered marked if v∈NG​(S)v\in N_{G}(S) or if v∉Sv\notin S and vv is isolated in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S). We note that a marked vertex may or may not be playable. A vertex is unmarked if it is not marked. At any given stage of the total isolation game, we define the sets SS, MM and UU as follows:

  1. ∙\bullet

    SS is the set of selected vertices.

  2. ∙\bullet

    MM is the set of marked vertices.

  3. ∙\bullet

    UU is the set of unmarked vertices.

We note that if uu is an unmarked vertex, then u∈Uu\in U and either u∈Su\in S and uu is an isolated vertex in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S) or uu belongs to a nontrivial component in the graph G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S). Thus every playable vertex in the total isolation game is adjacent to at least one unmarked vertex, and after such a vertex is played, at least one new vertex is marked. The game ends when all vertices of GG are marked.

Theorem 1

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and maximum degree Δ\Delta, then

ιgt​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−Δ−23​δ−2.\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{\Delta-2}{3\delta-2}.

Proof. Let GG be a connected graph of order nn with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and maximum degree Δ\Delta. As the D-game is played, let m2​i−1m_{2i-1} be the number of new vertices marked by Dominator on his iith move, and let m2​im_{2i} be the number of new vertices marked by Staller on her iith move. Upon completion of the game, say in tt moves, all vertices are marked implying that

n=∑i=1⌈t2⌉m2​i−1+∑i=1⌊t2⌋m2​i.n=\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil\frac{t}{2}\rceil}m_{2i-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{t}{2}\rfloor}m_{2i}. (1)

In what follows, let Dominator play according to a greedy strategy that on each of his moves he plays a vertex that results in a maximum increase in the number of marked vertices. That is, on each of his moves, Dominator plays a vertex that marks as many previously unmarked vertices as possible. Before Dominator’s first move, all vertices are unmarked, and so U=V⁡(G)U=V(G) and S=M=∅S=M=\emptyset. Let tt denote the number of moves played upon completion of the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy. We consider two stages in the game.

Stage 11.

A move of Dominator belongs to Stage 11 if there exists a playable move available to Dominator that marks at least two new vertices. A move of Staller belongs to Stage 11, if so does Dominator’s previous move.

Stage 22.

A move of Dominator belongs to Stage 22 if every playable move available to Dominator marks exactly one new vertex. A move of Staller belongs to Stage 22, if so does Dominator’s previous move.

As remarked earlier, Dominator plays according to a greedy strategy on each of his moves. We consider first the case when the game is complete in Stage 11.

Claim 1

If the game is complete in Stage 11, then t≤23​n−23​(Δ−2)t\leq\frac{2}{3}n-\frac{2}{3}(\Delta-2).

Proof. If Dominator plays a vertex vv of maximum degree Δ\Delta on his first move, then he marks at least Δ\Delta vertices, namely all Δ\Delta vertices in NG​(v)N_{G}(v) together with all isolated vertices in G−NG​(v)G-N_{G}(v) different from vv if such vertices exist. Thus there exists a playable move available to Dominator that marks at least Δ\Delta vertices. According to Dominator’s greedy strategy, we therefore infer that on his first move Dominator marks at least Δ\Delta vertices, and so m1≥Δ≥2m_{1}\geq\Delta\geq 2. Every playable move marks at least one new vertex. In particular, every move of Staller marks at least one new vertex, and so m2​i≥1m_{2i}\geq 1 for all i∈{1,…,⌊t/2⌋}i\in\{1,\ldots,\lfloor t/2\rfloor\}.

Suppose that Stage 1 consists of k1k_{1} moves of Dominator. Dominator’s first move marks at least Δ\Delta vertices and each of his remaining k1−1k_{1}-1 moves in Stage 1 mark at least two new vertices, and so m1≥Δm_{1}\geq\Delta and, if k1≥2k_{1}\geq 2, then m2​i−1≥2m_{2i-1}\geq 2 for all i∈[k1]∖{1}i\in[k_{1}]\setminus\{1\}. If the game is complete immediately after Dominator plays his k1thk_{1}^{\rm th} move, then t=2​k1−1t=2k_{1}-1 and, by Inequality (1) and our earlier observations, we have

n=∑i=1k1m2​i−1+∑i=1k1−1m2​i≥(2​k1+Δ−2)+(k1−1)=3​k1+Δ−3,n=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}-1}m_{2i}\geq(2k_{1}+\Delta-2)+(k_{1}-1)=3k_{1}+\Delta-3,

and so

t=2​k1−1=23​(n−Δ+3)−1<23​n−23​(Δ−2),t=2k_{1}-1=\frac{2}{3}(n-\Delta+3)-1<\frac{2}{3}n-\frac{2}{3}(\Delta-2),\vskip 2.84544pt

and so the desired upper bound in the statement of the claim holds (with strict inequality). Hence, we may assume that t≥2​k1t\geq 2k_{1}. If t=2​k1t=2k_{1}, then by Inequality (1) we have n≥(2​k1+Δ−2)+k1=3​k1+Δ−2n\geq(2k_{1}+\Delta-2)+k_{1}=3k_{1}+\Delta-2, and in this case

t=2​k1≤23​(n−Δ+2),t=2k_{1}\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-\Delta+2),

and so, once again, the desired upper bound in the statement of the claim holds. (□\Box)

Suppose, next, that the game is not complete in Stage 11 and that Stage 11 consists of k1k_{1} moves of Dominator. Thus, t>2​k1t>2k_{1}. In Stage 22 of the game, every playable move by either player marks exactly one new vertex. Suppose that k2k_{2} vertices in total are played in Stage 22 of the game, and so

t=2​k1+k2.t=2k_{1}+k_{2}. (2)

By our earlier assumptions, we have t>2​k1t>2k_{1}, and so k2≥1k_{2}\geq 1. We now consider the sets SS, MM and UU of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately after Stage 1 and before the game enters Stage 2. We proceed further by proving some structural properties that hold in the graph GG.

Claim 2

The following properties hold in the graph GG.

  1. (a)

    UU is an independent set in GG.

  2. (b)

    U⊆SU\subseteq S.

  3. (c)

    UU is a packing in GG.

Proof. (a) Suppose, to the contrary, that UU is not an independent set, and let CC be a nontrivial component in G⁡[U]G[U]. Suppose that |V⁡(C)|≥3|V(C)|\geq 3. In this case, the component CC contains a vertex, say vv, of degree at least 22 in CC. If Dominator plays the vertex vv, then he marks the neighbors of vv in CC and possibly some additional vertices not adjacent to vv. Such a move of Dominator therefore marks at least two new vertices, contradicting the fact that the game is in Stage 22. Hence, |V⁡(C)|=2|V(C)|=2, and so CC is a P2P_{2}-component in G⁡[U]G[U].

Let CC be the path u1​u2u_{1}u_{2}. If ui∈Su_{i}\in S, then the vertex u3−iu_{3-i} would be a marked vertex for i∈[2]i\in[2], a contradiction. Hence, neither u1u_{1} nor u2u_{2} belongs to the set SS. The graph GG is connected and Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2. Hence renaming vertices in the component CC if necessary, we may assume that degG⁡(u1)≥2\deg_{G}(u_{1})\geq 2. Let uu be a neighbor of u1u_{1} different from u2u_{2}. Necessarily, the vertex uu is marked but has not been selected. That is, u∈M∖Su\in M\setminus S. If Dominator plays the vertex uu, then he marks its neighbor u1u_{1} that belongs to CC. Furthermore, the vertex u2u_{2} now becomes isolated in the graph G−NG​(S∪{u})G-N_{G}(S\cup\{u\}) if u​u2∉E⁡(G)uu_{2}\notin E(G), and u2u_{2} becomes marked if u​u2∈E⁡(G)uu_{2}\in E(G). In either case, u2u_{2} becomes marked if Dominator plays uu. Therefore, Dominator marks at least two new vertices when he plays the vertex uu, contradicting the fact that the game is in Stage 22. This proves part (a).

(b) If there is a vertex, say xx, in UU that does not belong to the set SS, then x∉Sx\notin S and xx is isolated in G−NG​(S)G-N_{G}(S). However this would imply that the vertex xx is a marked vertex, a contradiction. Therefore, every vertex in UU belongs to the set SS, and so U⊆SU\subseteq S. This proves part (b).

(c) Suppose, to the contrary, that UU is not a packing in GG. Hence, since UU is an independent set, we infer that there exists two distinct vertices u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} in UU that have a common neighbor, say vv, in GG. Necessarily, the vertex vv is marked but has not been selected. If Dominator plays the vertex vv, then he marks both u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} and possibly some additional vertices. Such a move of Dominator therefore marks at least two new vertices, contradicting the fact that the game is in Stage 22. This proves part (c), and completes the proof of the claim. (□\Box)

By Claim 2(c), the set UU is a packing in GG and U⊆SU\subseteq S. We infer that every move played in Stage 22 marks exactly one vertex that belongs to the set UU. Let U={u1,…,uk2}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k_{2}}\} and let Bi=NG​(ui)B_{i}=N_{G}(u_{i}) for i∈[k2]i\in[k_{2}]. We note that the sets B1,…,Bk2B_{1},\ldots,B_{k_{2}} are pairwise vertex disjoint. We now let B=NG​(U)B=N_{G}(U), and so B=⋃i=1k2BiB=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k_{2}}B_{i} and

|B|=∑i=1k2|Bi|=∑i=1k2degG⁡(ui)≥δ​k2.|B|=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{2}}|B_{i}|=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{2}}\deg_{G}(u_{i})\geq\delta k_{2}. (3)

If the set BB contains a vertex that belongs to the set SS, then the neighbor of such a vertex that belongs to the set UU would be marked, a contradiction. Hence, B∩S=∅B\cap S=\emptyset.

Recall that by Equation (2), we have t=2​k1+k2t=2k_{1}+k_{2} where tt denote the number of moves played upon completion of the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy. Further recall that we are considering the sets SS, MM and UU of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately after Stage 1 and before the game enters Stage 2. Thus at this stage of the game, exactly 2​k12k_{1} vertices have been played.

Let AA be the set of vertices at distance at least 22 from every vertex in UU, and so A=V⁡(G)∖NG​[U]A=V(G)\setminus N_{G}[U]. Recall that U⊆SU\subseteq S and |U|=k2|U|=k_{2}, and so the set SS contains all k2k_{2} vertices in UU. Since B∩S=∅B\cap S=\emptyset, the 2​k1−k22k_{1}-k_{2} vertices in SS that do not belong to UU therefore belong to the set AA. Hence,

|A|≥|A∩S|=2​k1−k2.|A|\geq|A\cap S|=2k_{1}-k_{2}. (4)

Recall that by supposition δ≥2\delta\geq 2. We note that the sets AA, BB and UU are vertex disjoint and V⁡(G)=A∪B∪UV(G)=A\cup B\cup U. Thus, by Inequalities (3) and (4), and recalling that |U|=k2|U|=k_{2}, we have

k2=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1−k2)−δ​k2=n−2​k1−(δ−1)​k2,\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}-k_{2})-\delta k_{2}\\ &=&n-2k_{1}-(\delta-1)k_{2},\end{array}

and so (δ−1)​k2≤n−(2​k1+k2)=n−t(\delta-1)k_{2}\leq n-(2k_{1}+k_{2})=n-t, or, equivalently,

k2≤n−tδ−1.k_{2}\leq\frac{n-t}{\delta-1}. (5)

Immediately upon completion of Stage 11 of the game, we have

|M|=∑i=1k1m2​i−1+∑i=1k1m2​i≥(2​k1+Δ−2)+k1=3​k1+Δ−2.|M|=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}\geq(2k_{1}+\Delta-2)+k_{1}=3k_{1}+\Delta-2.

Recall that t=2​k1+k2t=2k_{1}+k_{2} by Equation (2), and so k1=12​(t−k2)k_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(t-k_{2}). From these observations and by Inequality (5), we have

n=|M|+|U|≥(3​k1+Δ−2)+k2=32​(t−k2)+k2+Δ−2=32​t−12​k2+Δ−2≥32​t−n−t2​(δ−1)+Δ−2,\begin{array}[]{lcl}n&=&|M|+|U|\\ &\geq&(3k_{1}+\Delta-2)+k_{2}\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}(t-k_{2})+k_{2}+\Delta-2\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}+\Delta-2\\ &\geq&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{n-t}{2(\delta-1)}+\Delta-2,\end{array}

or, equivalently,

(1+12​(δ−1))​n≥(32+12​(δ−1))​t+Δ−2.\left(1+\frac{1}{2(\delta-1)}\right)n\geq\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2(\delta-1)}\right)t+\Delta-2. (6)

Inequality (6) yields the simplified inequality

(2​δ−12​δ−2)​n≥(3​δ−22​δ−2)​t+Δ−2.\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{2\delta-2}\right)n\geq\left(\frac{3\delta-2}{2\delta-2}\right)t+\Delta-2. (7)

Solving for tt yields the inequality

t≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−Δ−23​δ−2.t\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{\Delta-2}{3\delta-2}. (8)

Recall that tt denotes the number of moves played in the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy. By Claim 1, if the game is complete in Stage 11, then t≤23​n−23​(Δ−2)t\leq\frac{2}{3}n-\frac{2}{3}(\Delta-2). If the game is not complete in Stage 11 and therefore enters Stage 22, then by Inequality (8) we have t≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−Δ−23​δ−2t\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{\Delta-2}{3\delta-2}. For n≥3n\geq 3 and n−1≥Δ≥δ≥2n-1\geq\Delta\geq\delta\geq 2, we note that

23​n−23​(Δ−2)<(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−Δ−23​δ−2.\frac{2}{3}n-\frac{2}{3}(\Delta-2)<\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{\Delta-2}{3\delta-2}.\vskip 2.84544pt

Hence, we have shown that Dominator’s greedy strategy is guaranteed to complete the total isolation game in at most (2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−Δ−23​δ−2\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{\Delta-2}{3\delta-2} moves, yielding the desired upper bound in the statement of the theorem. This completes the proof of Theorem 1. □\Box

If δ=Δ=2\delta=\Delta=2, then by Theorem 1 we have ιgt​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n. If δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3, then by Theorem 1 we have ιgt​(G)<(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)<\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n. Hence as an immediate consequence of Theorem 1, we obtain the following simplified upper bound on the game total isolation number.

Corollary 1

If GG is a connected graph of order nn with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then

ιgt​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n,\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n,

with strict inequality if the maximum degree Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3.

An analogous proof as in Theorem 1 yields the following upper bound on the Staller-start total isolation game. For completeness we provide the proof details.

Theorem 2

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then

ιgt′​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−(δ−1)​(2​δ−3)3​δ−2.\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{(\delta-1)(2\delta-3)}{3\delta-2}.

Proof. Let GG be a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and maximum degree Δ\Delta. Suppose that Δ=n−1\Delta=n-1. Thus, GG contains a dominating vertex, that is, a vertex adjacent to every other vertex. In this case, if Staller does not play a dominating vertex on her first move, then Dominator will do so, and complete the game in two moves. Hence, ιgt′​(G)=2\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)=2. Moreover since δ≤n−1\delta\leq n-1, we have 23​(n−δ+2)≥2\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2)\geq 2, and so ιgt′​(G)≤23​(n−δ+2)\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2). Hence we may assume that Δ≤n−2\Delta\leq n-2. In particular, n≥4n\geq 4. If n=4n=4, then G=C4G=C_{4} and ιgt′​(G)=2<23​(n−δ+2)\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)=2<\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2). Hence, we may further assume that n≥5n\geq 5.

As the game is played, let m2​im_{2i} be the number of new vertices marked by Dominator on his iith move, and let m2​i−1m_{2i-1} be the number of new vertices marked by Staller on her iith move. Upon completion of the game, all vertices are marked implying that

n=|M|=∑i=1⌊t2⌋m2​i+∑i=1⌈t2⌉m2​i−1.n=|M|=\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{t}{2}\rfloor}m_{2i}+\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil\frac{t}{2}\rceil}m_{2i-1}. (9)

In what follows, let Dominator play according to a greedy strategy that on each of his moves he plays a vertex that results in a maximum increase in the number of marked vertices. Before Staller’s first move, all vertices are unmarked, and so U=V⁡(G)U=V(G) and S=M=∅S=M=\emptyset. Let tt denote the number of moves played upon completion of the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy.

We consider Stage 11 and Stage 22 in the game as defined in the proof of Theorem 1. Suppose that Stage 1 consists of k1k_{1} moves of Dominator. Since n≥5n\geq 5 and Δ≤n−2\Delta\leq n-2 by assumption, we note that k1≥1k_{1}\geq 1. Each of Dominator’s k1k_{1} moves in Stage 1 mark at least two new vertices, and so m2​i≥2m_{2i}\geq 2 for all i∈[k1]i\in[k_{1}]. Staller’s first move marks at least δ\delta vertices and each of her remaining moves mark at least one new vertex.

Claim 3

If the game is complete in Stage 11, then t<23​(n−δ+2)t<\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2).

Proof. If the game is complete immediately after Dominator plays his k1thk_{1}^{\rm th} move, then Staller plays k1k_{1} moves in total, and so t=2​k1t=2k_{1} and, by Equation (9), we have

n=∑i=1k1m2​i+∑i=1k1m2​i−1≥2​k1+(δ+k1−1)=3​k1+δ−1,n=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}+\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i-1}\geq 2k_{1}+(\delta+k_{1}-1)=3k_{1}+\delta-1,

and so

t=2​k1=23​(n−δ+1)<23​(n−δ+2),t=2k_{1}=\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+1)<\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2),\vskip 2.84544pt

and so the desired upper bound in the statement of the claim holds. Hence, we may assume that t≥2​k1+1t\geq 2k_{1}+1. Since the game is complete in Stage 11, we infer that Staller plays k1+1k_{1}+1 moves and t=2​k1+1t=2k_{1}+1. By Equation (9), we have n≥2​k1+(δ+k1)=3​k1+δn\geq 2k_{1}+(\delta+k_{1})=3k_{1}+\delta, and in this case

t=2​k1+1≤23​(n−δ)+1<23​(n−δ+2),t=2k_{1}+1\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta)+1<\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2),\vskip 2.84544pt

and so, once again, the desired upper bound in the statement of the claim holds. (□\Box)

Suppose, next, that the game is not complete in Stage 11, and so the game enters Stage 22. Let Stage 11 consists of k1k_{1} moves of Dominator. In Stage 22 of the game, every playable move by either player marks exactly one new vertex. Suppose that k2k_{2} vertices in total are played in Stage 22 of the game, and so

t=2​k1+k2+1.t=2k_{1}+k_{2}+1. (10)

Claim 2 in the proof of Theorem 1 holds exactly as before. Defining the sets AA and BB as in the proof of Theorem 1, we have

|B|≥δ​k2and|A|≥2​k1+1−k2.|B|\geq\delta k_{2}\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{and}\hskip 14.22636pt|A|\geq 2k_{1}+1-k_{2}. (11)

By Inequality (11), and recalling that |U|=k2|U|=k_{2}, we have

k2=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1+1−k2)−δ​k2=n−(2​k1+1)−(δ−1)​k2,\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}+1-k_{2})-\delta k_{2}\\ &=&n-(2k_{1}+1)-(\delta-1)k_{2},\end{array}

and so (δ−1)​k2≤n−(2​k1+1+k2)=n−t(\delta-1)k_{2}\leq n-(2k_{1}+1+k_{2})=n-t, or, equivalently,

k2≤n−tδ−1.k_{2}\leq\frac{n-t}{\delta-1}. (12)

Immediately upon completion of Stage 11 of the game, we have

|M|=∑i=1k1m2​i+∑i=1k1+1m2​i−1≥2​k1+(δ+k1)=3​k1+δ.|M|=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}+\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}+1}m_{2i-1}\geq 2k_{1}+(\delta+k_{1})=3k_{1}+\delta.

Recall that t=2​k1+1+k2t=2k_{1}+1+k_{2} by Equation (10), and so k1=12​(t−k2−1)k_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(t-k_{2}-1). From these observations and by Inequality (12), we have

n=|M|+|U|≥(3​k1+δ)+k2=32​(t−k2−1)+k2+δ=32​t−12​k2+δ−32≥32​t−n−t2​(δ−1)+δ−32,\begin{array}[]{lcl}n&=&|M|+|U|\\ &\geq&(3k_{1}+\delta)+k_{2}\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}(t-k_{2}-1)+k_{2}+\delta\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}+\delta-\frac{3}{2}\\ &\geq&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{n-t}{2(\delta-1)}+\delta-\frac{3}{2},\end{array}

or, equivalently,

(2​δ−12​δ−2)​n≥(3​δ−22​δ−2)​t+δ−32.\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{2\delta-2}\right)n\geq\left(\frac{3\delta-2}{2\delta-2}\right)t+\delta-\frac{3}{2}. (13)

Solving for tt yields the inequality

t≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−(δ−1)​(2​δ−3)3​δ−2.t\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{(\delta-1)(2\delta-3)}{3\delta-2}.\vskip 2.84544pt (14)

Recall that tt denotes the number of moves played in the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy. By Claim 3, if the game is complete in Stage 11, then t<23​(n−δ+2)t<\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2). If the game is not complete in Stage 11 and therefore enters Stage 22, then by Inequality (14) we have t≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−(δ−1)​(2​δ−3)3​δ−2t\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{(\delta-1)(2\delta-3)}{3\delta-2}. For n≥3n\geq 3 and n−1≥δ≥2n-1\geq\delta\geq 2, we note that

23​(n−δ+2)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−(δ−1)​(2​δ−3)3​δ−2.\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+2)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{(\delta-1)(2\delta-3)}{3\delta-2}.\vskip 2.84544pt

Hence, we have shown that Dominator’s greedy strategy is guaranteed to complete the total isolation game in at most (2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−(δ−1)​(2​δ−3)3​δ−2\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{(\delta-1)(2\delta-3)}{3\delta-2} moves, yielding the desired upper bound in the statement of the theorem. This completes the proof of Theorem 2. □\Box

If δ=2\delta=2, then by Theorem 2 we have ιgt′​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−14\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{1}{4}.

If δ≥3\delta\geq 3, then by Theorem 2 we have ιgt′​(G)<(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−14\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)<\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{1}{4}.

Hence as an immediate consequence of Theorem 2, we obtain the following simplified upper bound on the Staller-start game total isolation number.

Corollary 2

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then

ιgt′​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−14,\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{1}{4},

with strict inequality if δ≥3\delta\geq 3.

For δ≥2\delta\geq 2, we note that 2​δ−13​δ−2≤34\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\leq\frac{3}{4} (with strict inequality if δ≥3\delta\geq 3). Hence, Corollary 1 and Corollary 2 yield the following upper bounds on the (Dominator-start) game total isolation number and Staller-start game total isolation number of a graph with minimum degree at least 22.

Corollary 3

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, then the following hold.

  1. (a)

    ιgt​(G)≤34​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{3}{4}n.

  2. (b)

    ιgt′​(G)≤34​n−14\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{4}.

3.1 Graphs with diameter two

Let GG be a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥2\delta\geq 2. By Corollary 1, ιgt​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n and by Corollary 3, ιgt′​(G)≤(2​δ−13​δ−2)​n−14\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\left(\frac{2\delta-1}{3\delta-2}\right)n-\frac{1}{4}. Hence if δ\delta tends to infinity, then the upper bound on ιgt​(G)\iota_{\rm gt}(G) tends to 23​n\frac{2}{3}n and the upper bound on ιgt′​(G)\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G) tends to 23​n−14\frac{2}{3}n-\frac{1}{4}.

As a consequence of our proof of Theorem 1, we show that the (Dominator-start) game total isolation number and Staller-start game total isolation numbers for connected graphs of order n≥3n\geq 3 and diameter at most 22 is at most 23​n\frac{2}{3}n. We remark that it is well-known that almost every graph has diameter 22 by a property of the Erdős-Rényi random graph model. Hence by Theorem 3 below, almost every graph GG satisfies ιgt​(G)≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n and ιgt′​(G)≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n

Theorem 3

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with diam⁡(G)≤2{\rm diam}(G)\leq 2, then

ιgt​(G)≤23​nandιgt′​(G)≤23​n.\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{and}\hskip 14.22636pt\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n.

Proof. Let GG be a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with diam⁡(G)≤2{\rm diam}(G)\leq 2. Further, let GG have minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥1\delta\geq 1 and maximum degree Δ\Delta. If G=KnG=K_{n}, then 2=ιgt​(G)≤23​n2=\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n and 2=ιgt′​(G)≤23​n2=\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n. Thus, we assume that diam⁡(G)=2{\rm diam}(G)=2, which implies that Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2.

Suppose that δ=1\delta=1. Let v1v_{1} be a vertex of degree 11 in GG and let vv be its (unique) neighbor. Since diam⁡(G)=2{\rm diam}(G)=2, we note that V​(G)=NG​[v]V(G)=N_{G}[v], and so degG⁡(v)=Δ=n−1\deg_{G}(v)=\Delta=n-1. Thus, GG contains a dominating vertex, namely vv. In the D-game, if Dominator plays the vertex vv on his first move, he marks all vertices of GG different from vv. Since one additional move completes the game, we have ιgt​(G)=2≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)=2\leq\frac{2}{3}n. In the S-game, if Staller plays the dominating vertex vv, then one additional move of Dominator completes the game, and if Staller does not play the vertex vv on her first move, then Dominator plays the vertex vv on his first move, and once again the game is complete in two moves. Hence, ιgt′​(G)=2≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)=2\leq\frac{2}{3}n. Hence we may assume that δ≥2\delta\geq 2.

Suppose that Δ=2\Delta=2. Since diam⁡(G)=2{\rm diam}(G)=2, we infer that G∈{C4,C5}G\in\{C_{4},C_{5}\}. Since ιgt​(C4)=2\iota_{\rm gt}(C_{4})=2 and ιgt​(C5)=3\iota_{\rm gt}(C_{5})=3, we have that ιgt​(G)<23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)<\frac{2}{3}n. Moreover since ιgt′​(C4)=2\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(C_{4})=2 and ιgt′​(C5)=2\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(C_{5})=2, we have that ιgt​(G)<23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)<\frac{2}{3}n. Hence we may further assume that Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3.

Suppose firstly that we are in the D-game. In this case, we adopt the notation and proof of Theorem 1. In particular, tt denotes the number of moves played in the D-game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy, and so ιgt​(G)≤t\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq t. We show that t≤23​nt\leq\frac{2}{3}n. By our earlier assumptions, δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3. By Claim 2 in the proof of Theorem 1 we have that U⊆SU\subseteq S and UU is a packing in GG. If |U|≥2|U|\geq 2, then diam⁡(G)≥3{\rm diam}(G)\geq 3, a contradiction. Hence, k2=|U|≤1k_{2}=|U|\leq 1. Suppose that k2=0k_{2}=0. Thus, the game is completed in Stage 11, and t=2​k1−1t=2k_{1}-1 or t=2​k1t=2k_{1}. If t=2​k1−1t=2k_{1}-1, then as shown in the proof of Stage 11 of Theorem 1 we have t<23​nt<\frac{2}{3}n. Hence, we may assume that t=2​k1t=2k_{1}. Recall that m2​i−1≥2m_{2i-1}\geq 2 for all i∈[k1]i\in[k_{1}] and m2​i≥1m_{2i}\geq 1 for all i∈[k1]i\in[k_{1}]. As shown in the proof of Theorem 1 following Dominator’s greedy strategy we have m1≥Δm_{1}\geq\Delta, and so m1≥3m_{1}\geq 3. Thus,

n=(m1+∑i=2k1m2​i−1)+(∑i=1k1m2​i)≥(2​k1+1)+k1=3​k1+1,n=\left(m_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{k_{1}}m_{2i-1}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}\right)\geq(2k_{1}+1)+k_{1}=3k_{1}+1,

and so, t=2​k1≤23​(n−1)<23​nt=2k_{1}\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-1)<\frac{2}{3}n. Hence we may assume that k2=1k_{2}=1, for otherwise the desired upper bound follows. In this case, we have t=2​k1+k2=2​k1+1t=2k_{1}+k_{2}=2k_{1}+1, and so

n=(m1+∑i=2k1m2​i−1)+(∑i=1k1m2​i)+k2≥(2​k1+1)+k1+1=3​k1+2,n=\left(m_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{k_{1}}m_{2i-1}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}\right)+k_{2}\geq(2k_{1}+1)+k_{1}+1=3k_{1}+2,

implying that t=2​k1+1≤23​(n−2)+1<23​nt=2k_{1}+1\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-2)+1<\frac{2}{3}n.

Suppose secondly that we are in the S-game. In this case, we adopt the notation and proof of Theorem 2. In particular, tt denotes the number of moves played in the S-game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy, and so ιgt​(G)≤t\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq t. By our earlier assumptions, δ≥2\delta\geq 2 and Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3. We show that t≤23​nt\leq\frac{2}{3}n. As in the case of the D-game we have that U⊆SU\subseteq S. Further, the set UU is a packing in GG and k2=|U|≤1k_{2}=|U|\leq 1. Suppose that k2=0k_{2}=0. Thus, the game is completed in Stage 11, and t=2​k1t=2k_{1} or t=2​k1+1t=2k_{1}+1. If t=2​k1t=2k_{1}, then as shown in the proof of Theorem 2 we have t≤23​(n−δ+1)<23​nt\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-\delta+1)<\frac{2}{3}n noting that δ≥2\delta\geq 2. Hence, we may assume that t=2​k1+1t=2k_{1}+1. Recall that m1≥δ≥2m_{1}\geq\delta\geq 2 and m2​i−1≥1m_{2i-1}\geq 1 for all i∈[k1+1]∖{1}i\in[k_{1}+1]\setminus\{1\}, and m2​i≥2m_{2i}\geq 2 for all i∈[k1]i\in[k_{1}]. Thus,

n=(∑i=1k1m2​i)+(m1+∑i=2k1+1m2​i−1)≥2​k1+(2+k1)=3​k1+2,n=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}\right)+\left(m_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{k_{1}+1}m_{2i-1}\right)\geq 2k_{1}+(2+k_{1})=3k_{1}+2,

and so, t=2​k1+1≤23​(n−2)+1<23​nt=2k_{1}+1\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-2)+1<\frac{2}{3}n. Hence we may assume that k2=1k_{2}=1, for otherwise the desired upper bound follows. In this case, we have t=2​k1+1+k2=2​k1+2t=2k_{1}+1+k_{2}=2k_{1}+2, and so

n=(∑i=1k1m2​i)+(m1+∑i=1k1+1m2​i−1)+k2≥2​k1+(2+k1)+1=3​k1+3,n=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}}m_{2i}\right)+\left(m_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k_{1}+1}m_{2i-1}\right)+k_{2}\geq 2k_{1}+(2+k_{1})+1=3k_{1}+3,

implying that t=2​k1+2≤23​(n−3)+2=23​nt=2k_{1}+2\leq\frac{2}{3}(n-3)+2=\frac{2}{3}n. □\Box

4 General upper bounds for connected graphs

We consider next general upper bounds on the (Dominator-start) game total isolation number and Staller-start game total isolation number of a connected graph.

Theorem 4

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3, then ιgt​(G)<56​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)<\frac{5}{6}n.

Proof. Let GG be a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥1\delta\geq 1 and maximum degree Δ\Delta. If δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then the desired bound follows from Corollary 1. If diam⁡(G)≤2{\rm diam}(G)\leq 2, then the desired bound follows from Theorem 3. Hence we may assume that δ=1\delta=1 and that the connected graph GG satisfies diam⁡(G)≥3{\rm diam}(G)\geq 3. In what follows we adopt the notation and proof of Theorem 1. In particular, tt denotes the number of moves played in the game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy, and so ιgt​(G)≤t\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq t.

We now modify Dominator’s strategy as follows. As in the proof of Theorem 1, Dominator plays according to a greedy strategy, and so on each of his moves, Dominator plays a vertex that marks as many previously unmarked vertices as possible. Subject to Dominator playing according to his greedy strategy, Dominator selects a non-leaf on each of his moves whenever possible. Thus if Dominator has two or more greedy moves available to play (each marking the same number of previously unmarked vertices), then Dominator selects among all such greedy moves a non-leaf if at all possible. We show that with the modified strategy, we have t≤56​nt\leq\frac{5}{6}n.

Consider the sets SS, MM and UU of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately after Stage 1 and before the game enters Stage 2. By Claim 2 in the proof of Theorem 1 we have that U⊆SU\subseteq S and UU is a packing in GG. Recall that k2=|U|k_{2}=|U|. If k2=0k_{2}=0, then the game is completed in Stage 11, and t=2​k1−1t=2k_{1}-1 or t=2​k1t=2k_{1}. In both cases, as shown in the proof of Stage 11 of Theorem 1 we have t≤23​nt\leq\frac{2}{3}n. Hence, we may assume that k2≥1k_{2}\geq 1.

Adopting our earlier notation in the proof of Theorem 1, let U={u1,…,uk2}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k_{2}}\} and let Bi=NG​(ui)B_{i}=N_{G}(u_{i}) for i∈[k2]i\in[k_{2}]. As before, let B=NG​(U)B=N_{G}(U). Renaming vertices in UU if necessary, we may assume degG⁡(u1)≤degG⁡(u2)≤⋯≤degG⁡(uk2)\deg_{G}(u_{1})\leq\deg_{G}(u_{2})\leq\cdots\leq\deg_{G}(u_{k_{2}}). Let U1U_{1} be the subset of vertices in UU of degree 11 in GG, and let U2=U∖U1U_{2}=U\setminus U_{1}, and so every vertex in U2U_{2} has degree at least 22 in GG. Further, let |Ui|=ni|U_{i}|=n_{i} for i∈[2]i\in[2]. If n1=0n_{1}=0, then U=U2U=U_{2} and

|B|=∑i=1k2degG⁡(ui)≥2​k2.|B|=\sum_{i=1}^{k_{2}}\deg_{G}(u_{i})\geq 2k_{2}. (15)

Recall that by Inequality (4) in the proof of Theorem 1 we have |A|≥2​k1−k2|A|\geq 2k_{1}-k_{2}. Together with Inequality (15) this yields

k2=|U|=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1−k2)−2​k2=n−(2​k1+k2)=n−t.\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}\,=\,|U|&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}-k_{2})-2k_{2}\\ &=&n-(2k_{1}+k_{2})\\ &=&n-t.\end{array}

Thus,

n=|M|+|U|≥3​k1+k2=32​(t−k2)+k2=32​t−12​k2≥32​t−12​(n−t),\begin{array}[]{lcl}n\,=\,|M|+|U|&\geq&3k_{1}+k_{2}\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}(t-k_{2})+k_{2}\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}\\ &\geq&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}(n-t),\end{array}

or, equivalently, t≤34​nt\leq\frac{3}{4}n. Hence we may assume that n1≥1n_{1}\geq 1.

k1≥n1k_{1}\geq n_{1}. Proof. Let uu be an arbitrary vertex in U1U_{1}. Thus, degG⁡(u)=1\deg_{G}(u)=1. Let vv be the (unique) neighbor of uu. By assumption, diam⁡(G)≥3{\rm diam}(G)\geq 3, implying that vv has a neighbor, say ww, of degree at least 22 in GG. By our earlier observations, U1⊆U⊆SU_{1}\subseteq U\subseteq S and UU is a packing in GG. Moreover, k2=|U|k_{2}=|U|. Recall that SS, MM and UU denote the sets of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately after Stage 1 and before the game enters Stage 2. In particular, we note that all vertices in UU were played in Stage 11 of the game.

We show that the vertex u∈U1u\in U_{1} was played by Staller (in Stage 11 of the game). Suppose, to the contrary, that Dominator played the vertex uu in Stage 11 of the game. Let S′S^{\prime}, M′M^{\prime}, and U′U^{\prime} denote the sets of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately before vertex uu is played. Then, u∉S′u\notin S^{\prime} and v∈U′v\in U^{\prime}. Also, since uu is unmarked at the end of Stage 11, it follows that u∈U′u\in U^{\prime}. However if Dominator had played the vertex ww instead of the vertex uu, then he would have marked all the new vertices that were marked when playing the vertex uu, except possibly for the vertex ww (which may become marked when the vertex uu is played), and in addition he would have marked the vertex uu. Hence, Dominator would have marked at least as many vertices by playing the vertex ww instead of playing the vertex uu. However since uu is a leaf and ww is a non-leaf, according to Dominator’s modified strategy he would have played the vertex ww, a contradiction. Hence the vertex uu must have been played by Staller in Stage 11 of the game. Moreover when the vertex uu was played by Staller, Dominator’s previous (greedy) move necessary marked at least two new vertices, noting that playing the vertex ww would mark at least two new vertices, namely uu and vv.

The vertices in the set U1U_{1} were therefore all selected by Staller. Since every move of Staller that played a vertex in U1U_{1} was played in Stage 1 of the game and since Staller played a total of k1k_{1} moves in Stage 1 of the game, we infer that n1≤k1n_{1}\leq k_{1}. (□\Box)

k2≤12​(n−k1)k_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}(n-k_{1}). Proof. By assumption, n1≥1n_{1}\geq 1. Thus,

|B|=∑i=1n1|Bi|+∑i=n1+1k2|Bi|≥n1+2​(k2−n1)=2​k2−n1.|B|=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}}|B_{i}|+\sum_{i=n_{1}+1}^{k_{2}}|B_{i}|\geq n_{1}+2(k_{2}-n_{1})=2k_{2}-n_{1}. (16)

Recall that by Inequality (4) in the proof of Theorem 1 we have |A|≥2​k1−k2|A|\geq 2k_{1}-k_{2}. By Claim A, we have k1≥n1k_{1}\geq n_{1}. Together with Inequality (16) these observations yield the inequality chain given by

k2=|U|=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1−k2)−(2​k2−n1)=n−2​k1−k2+n1≤n−k1−k2,\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}\,=\,|U|&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}-k_{2})-(2k_{2}-n_{1})\\ &=&n-2k_{1}-k_{2}+n_{1}\\ &\leq&n-k_{1}-k_{2},\end{array}

or, equivalently, k2≤12​(n−k1)k_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}(n-k_{1}). (□\Box)

Recall that n≥32​t−12​k2n\geq\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}. Hence by Claim B, we infer that n≥32​t−14​(n−k1)n\geq\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{4}(n-k_{1}), or, equivalently, t≤56​n−16​k1t\leq\frac{5}{6}n-\frac{1}{6}k_{1}. Since k1≥1k_{1}\geq 1, we have t<56​nt<\frac{5}{6}n, as claimed. This completes the proof of Theorem 4. □\Box

Theorem 5

If GG is a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3, then ιgt′​(G)≤56​n\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{5}{6}n.

Proof. Let GG be a connected graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with minimum degree δ\delta where δ≥1\delta\geq 1 and maximum degree Δ\Delta. If δ≥2\delta\geq 2, then by Corollary 3 we have ιgt′​(G)≤34​n−14<56​n\iota_{\rm gt}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{4}<\frac{5}{6}n. If diam⁡(G)≤2{\rm diam}(G)\leq 2, then the desired bound follows from Theorem 3. Hence we may assume that δ=1\delta=1 and that the connected graph GG satisfies diam⁡(G)≥3{\rm diam}(G)\geq 3. In what follows we adopt the notation and proof of Theorem 2. In particular, tt denotes the number of moves played in the S-game when Dominator adopts his greedy strategy, and so ιgt​(G)≤t\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq t.

We now modify Dominator’s strategy as follows. As in the proof of Theorem 3, Dominator plays according to a greedy strategy, and so on each of his moves, Dominator plays a vertex that marks as many previously unmarked vertices as possible. Subject to Dominator playing according to his greedy strategy, Dominator selects a non-leaf on each of his moves whenever possible. Thus if Dominator has two or more greedy moves available to play (each marking the same number of previously unmarked vertices), then Dominator selects among all such greedy moves a non-leaf if at all possible. We show that with the modified strategy, we have t≤56​nt\leq\frac{5}{6}n.

Consider the sets SS, MM and UU of selected, marked and unmarked vertices immediately after Stage 1 and before the game enters Stage 2. By Claim 2 in the proof of Theorem 1 we have that U⊆SU\subseteq S and UU is a packing in GG. Recall that k2=|U|k_{2}=|U|. If k2=0k_{2}=0, then the game is completed in Stage 11, and t=2​k1t=2k_{1} or t=2​k1+1t=2k_{1}+1. In both cases, as shown in the proof of Stage 11 of Theorem 2 we have t≤23​n+13t\leq\frac{2}{3}n+\frac{1}{3} noting that δ=1\delta=1. Hence, we may assume that k2≥1k_{2}\geq 1.

We now adopt our earlier notation for the set AA and BB as in the proof of Theorem 2 and for the sets UU, U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} in the proof of Theorem 4. In particular, |Ui|=ni|U_{i}|=n_{i} for i∈[2]i\in[2]. If n1=0n_{1}=0, then U=U2U=U_{2} and, as in the proof of Theorem 2, we infer in this case that

|B|≥2​k2and|A|≥2​k1+1−k2.|B|\geq 2k_{2}\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{and}\hskip 14.22636pt|A|\geq 2k_{1}+1-k_{2}. (17)

By Inequality (17), and recalling that |U|=k2|U|=k_{2}, we have

k2=|U|=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1+1−k2)−2​k2=n−(2​k1+1+k2)=n−t.\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}\,=\,|U|&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}+1-k_{2})-2k_{2}\\ &=&n-(2k_{1}+1+k_{2})\\ &=&n-t.\end{array}

Thus,

n=|M|+|U|≥(3​k1+1)+k2=32​(t−k2−1)+k2+1=32​t−12​k2−12≥32​t−12​(n−t)−12,\begin{array}[]{lcl}n\,=\,|M|+|U|&\geq&(3k_{1}+1)+k_{2}\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}(t-k_{2}-1)+k_{2}+1\\ &=&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}-\frac{1}{2}\\ &\geq&\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}(n-t)-\frac{1}{2},\end{array}

or, equivalently, t≤34​n+14t\leq\frac{3}{4}n+\frac{1}{4}. Hence we may assume that n1≥1n_{1}\geq 1. Proceeding now exactly as in the proof of Theorem 4 (see Claim A), we have k1≥n1k_{1}\geq n_{1} and |B|≥2​k1−n1|B|\geq 2k_{1}-n_{1}. We therefore infer that

k2=|U|=n−|A|−|B|≤n−(2​k1+1−k2)−(2​k2−n1)=n−k1−k2−1+(n1−k1)≤n−k1−k2−1,\begin{array}[]{lcl}k_{2}\,=\,|U|&=&n-|A|-|B|\\ &\leq&n-(2k_{1}+1-k_{2})-(2k_{2}-n_{1})\\ &=&n-k_{1}-k_{2}-1+(n_{1}-k_{1})\\ &\leq&n-k_{1}-k_{2}-1,\end{array}

or, equivalently, k2≤12​(n−k1−1)k_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}(n-k_{1}-1). As shown earlier, we have n≥32​t−12​k2−12n\geq\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}-\frac{1}{2}. Hence, n≥32​t−12​k2−12≥32​t−14​(n−k1−1)−12n\geq\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{2}k_{2}-\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{3}{2}t-\frac{1}{4}(n-k_{1}-1)-\frac{1}{2}, or, equivalently, t≤56​n−16​(k1+1)+13t\leq\frac{5}{6}n-\frac{1}{6}(k_{1}+1)+\frac{1}{3}. Since k1≥1k_{1}\geq 1, we have t≤56​nt\leq\frac{5}{6}n, as claimed. This completes the proof of Theorem 5. □\Box

5 Closing comments

We pose the following 23\frac{2}{3}-conjecture for the game total isolation number.

Conjecture 1

If GG is a graph of order nn and every component of GG has order at least 33, then ιgt​(G)≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n.

We remark that if Conjecture 1 is true, then the 23​n\frac{2}{3}n-upper bound on the game total isolation number is best possible. As an example, let GG be a graph of order nn where every component is a path P3P_{3}- or P6P_{6}-component or a cycle C3C_{3}- or C6C_{6}-component. Staller’s strategy is to reply to every move of Dominator by playing in the component that Dominator played in on his previous move. When Dominator plays in a P3P_{3}- or C3C_{3}-component, Staller responds with a playable vertex in that component that marks all vertices. When Dominator plays in a P6P_{6}- or C6C_{6}-component, Staller responds by playing a playable vertex in that component following her optimal strategy, thereby ensuring that four moves (two by Dominator and two by Staller) are played in such components. (Note that if Dominator plays a vertex vv from a C6C_{6}-component CC, then Staller plays the vertex at distance 33 from vv on the cycle CC, thereby forcing two additional moves played on CC.) Upon completion of the game, two moves are played in every P3P_{3}- and C3C_{3}-component and four moves are played in every P6P_{6}- and C6C_{6}-component, implying that ιgt​(G)≥23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\geq\frac{2}{3}n. However if Conjecture 1 is true, then ιgt​(G)≤23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)\leq\frac{2}{3}n. Consequently, ιgt​(G)=23​n\iota_{\rm gt}(G)=\frac{2}{3}n.
